general-cold-at-night.question: Wait… is it really cold at night?
general-cold-at-night.answer: Yes — even in summer. Desert nights drop fast after sunset. Bring layers. We’re not kidding.

general-never-ridden-camel.question: What if I’ve never ridden a camel?
general-never-ridden-camel.answer: Neither had most of our travelers. The camels are calm, the pace is slow, and our guides walk beside you the whole way.

general-with-kids.question: Can I do this with kids?
general-with-kids.answer: Absolutely. Families join every week. The minibus, camp beds, and meals all work for children, and the camel trek is short and gentle.

general-bathrooms-at-camp.question: Are there bathrooms at the camp?
general-bathrooms-at-camp.answer: Yes. Shared bathrooms come standard; Comfort and Superior camps include a private bathroom inside your tent.

general-wifi.question: Will there be Wi-Fi? Be honest.
general-wifi.answer: Barely, and that’s kind of the point. There’s patchy signal at camp — enough for a quick message, not for doom-scrolling.

general-solo-traveler.question: I’m a solo traveler. Will I feel out of place?
general-solo-traveler.answer: Not at all. Roughly a third of our travelers come solo. Shared dinners around the fire make it easy to meet people.

general-if-it-rains.question: What if it rains?
general-if-it-rains.answer: Rain in the Sahara is rare, but the itinerary flexes if weather turns. Your guide adjusts stops so you never miss the highlights.

general-how-far-in-advance.question: How far in advance should I book?
general-how-far-in-advance.answer: Two to four weeks is comfortable in peak season (Sep–Nov, Mar–May). Off-season, a few days is often enough.

general-cancellation-policy.question: What’s your cancellation policy?
general-cancellation-policy.answer: Free cancellation up to 48 hours before departure for a full refund. Inside 48 hours we’ll rebook you or refund 50%.

general-riad-airport-pickup.question: Can you pick me up from my riad or the airport?
general-riad-airport-pickup.answer: Yes. Riad pickup in Marrakech is included. Airport pickup can be arranged — just tell us your flight details.

booking-need-to-cancel.question: What if I need to cancel?
booking-need-to-cancel.answer: Free cancellation up to 48 hours before departure. After that, 50% refund. We get it though — email or WhatsApp us, we're human.

booking-when-charged.question: When am I charged?
booking-when-charged.answer: You pay 20% now to book your spot. The rest is due 48 hours before departure — by card, bank transfer or cash on arrival.

booking-pickup.question: What about pickup?
booking-pickup.answer: We pick you up directly from your Riad or Hotel in Marrakech (or Fez, depending on your route) at the time confirmed the day before departure.

booking-change-date.question: Can I change my date after booking?
booking-change-date.answer: Yes — free of charge up to 48 hours before departure, subject to availability. Just message us on WhatsApp.

booking-group-changes.question: What if my group changes?
booking-group-changes.answer: No problem. Let us know the new number of travelers as early as possible and we'll adjust your quote and camp arrangements.

grand-crossing-day-1.title: The Mountains Will Test You
grand-crossing-day-1.paragraphs:
We leave Marrakech early. The chaos of the medina fades behind us as we climb the High Atlas — switchback after switchback, Berber villages clinging to the rock, snow on the peaks until late spring.

We stop in Ait Ben Haddou — the UNESCO kasbah where Gladiator, Game of Thrones, and a hundred other films were shot. We eat with a view. We pass through Ouarzazate, Morocco’s “Hollywood of Africa.”

By evening, we’re deep in the Dades Valley — red cliffs, palm groves, your first real Moroccan dinner. You’ll sleep well. You’ll need it.

grand-crossing-day-2.title: Into the Great Sahara
grand-crossing-day-2.paragraphs:
Morning light fills the Dades, then the road coils into Todra Gorge — 300-metre rust-red walls closing in until the sky is just a ribbon overhead.

At the edge of Erg Chebbi we trade the van for camels. An hour into the dunes the last rooftop vanishes — there is only sand, wind, and the slow sway of the caravan.

Camp is a ring of black Berber tents in a hollow between dunes. Tagine under the stars, drums after dark, and a 2am silence you will never forget.

grand-crossing-day-3.title: Where the Past Still Lives
grand-crossing-day-3.paragraphs:
We leave the desert and climb into the Middle Atlas — cedar forests, Barbary macaques at the roadside, and Ifrane, a town that looks airlifted from the Alps.

By afternoon we reach Fes. We step into the medina — 9,000 lanes, no cars, donkeys hauling everything — and twelve centuries close over our heads.

We watch the tanneries from a rooftop, eat where the locals eat, and lose ourselves on purpose. Most travelers wish they’d booked another day here.

about-story.heading: Born under the stars.
about-story.body:
I grew up in the Moroccan Sahara. The dunes were my playground. The stars were my nightlight. Mint tea by a fire was just how every evening ended. As a kid, I thought every grandmother told stories under that many stars. I thought every road home crossed a sea of sand.

It took leaving to realize that wasn’t a normal childhood. That the silence I knew, the hospitality I grew up with, and a sky so full of stars they look fake — most people never get to feel any of it. Not once. And the few who do come are often hurried past the best parts of it.

So in 2017, I started Budget Desert Tour. The mission is simple: share the Sahara I grew up in with travelers who want more than a photo. Small groups. Real Berber families. Honest prices. Three days slow enough to put your camera down, sit with people, eat what they eat, and let the silence work on you the way it worked on me.

Come and see. We’ll take you across the Atlas. We’ll bring you to a real Berber camp tucked into the dunes. You’ll sleep under stars so close you’ll instinctively reach for them. And when the silence really lands — usually somewhere after dinner on Night 1 — you’ll know exactly what I mean. ☺
about-story.quote: “I’m not selling the Sahara. I’m sharing the Morocco I fell in love with. ♥♥♥”
about-story.author: Fatima

about-partners.heading: Local partners, every step of the way.
about-partners.body:
From the first night to the last, you stay with our local partners, small hotels along the route and Berber families running camps in the heart of the Sahara.

These are people from the region, doing business in the place they know best. The hotel in Dades Valley. The camps in the middle of the Erg Chebbi dunes. We’ve been working with the same partners for years, and we choose them for one simple reason: they do things right.
about-partners.body_secondary:
What you get from these partnerships is the real thing. Nights in the middle of the desert, not on its edge. By day, dunes rolling out in every direction. At sunset, sand turning gold, then copper, then red. By night, a silence so complete you can hear the fire, and a sky no city can show you.

Book with us, and you stay with them. That’s the arrangement.
about-partners.statement:
That’s what “authentic” actually means.
Not a marketing word.
A relationship.

about-hero.body: Born in the south. Raised on the dunes. Tired of watching tourists pay €300 for a piece of the place we call home.
about-hero.heading_lines:
We’re a few people from
the Sahara, sharing it with you.

about-supports.body:
When you book with us, your money does two things:

First, it supports the Berber families we partner with in the dunes. The cooks who make your tagine. The musicians who drum by the fire. The hosts who keep the camp running. These aren’t employees of a hotel chain — they’re independent families, and we work with them as equals. Fair rates. Long-term partnerships. On-time payments.

Second, it supports our small team here in Marrakech. The drivers who get you safely across the Atlas. Our office staff. The people who answer your WhatsApp messages at midnight when you’re stressed about whether to pack a jacket.

No corporate owners skimming a cut to a Paris boardroom. No investors expecting 30% margins. Just two groups of Moroccans — one in the desert, one in the city — making a real living by sharing what we love about this country.

That’s what “local” means to us.
about-supports.statement:
We’re not getting rich on this.
We’re getting to share where we’re from.
That’s the point.
